facts.text: A Safety Integrity Level is a grade from 1 to 4 in the IEC 61508 family specifying the risk reduction a safety function must deliver; the acronym SIL also means software-in-the-loop, a different concept.
facts.quote: A Safety Integrity Level is a grade from 1 to 4 used in the IEC 61508 family of standards to say how much risk reduction a safety function must deliver, and the same three letters are used in this booklet for software-in-the-loop, a completely different thing.

facts.text: IEC 61508 is the general standard for electrical, electronic and programmable safety systems, used in process plants and railways and, through IEC 62061, in machinery.
facts.quote: IEC 61508 is the general standard for electrical, electronic and programmable safety systems, used in process plants, railways and, through IEC 62061, in machinery.

facts.text: IEC 61508 grades safety functions from SIL 1, the lowest grade, to SIL 4, the highest grade.
facts.quote: It grades safety functions from SIL 1 (lowest) to SIL 4 (highest).

facts.text: For safety functions that act often, each Safety Integrity Level specifies a band of probability of dangerous failure per hour; SIL 1 allows between one dangerous failure in 100,000 hours and one in a million hours.
facts.quote: For a function that acts often, each grade is a band of probability of dangerous failure per hour: SIL 1 allows between one dangerous failure in 100,000 hours and one in a million

facts.text: For safety functions that act often, each higher Safety Integrity Level is ten times stricter; SIL 3 has a dangerous-failure probability band between 10^-8 and 10^-7 per hour and is roughly as demanding as PL e.
facts.quote: each higher grade is ten times stricter, so SIL 3 (between 10^-8 and 10^-7 per hour) is roughly as demanding as PL e.

facts.text: The Safety Integrity Level also sets how rigorously hardware must be analyzed and software developed.
facts.quote: The grade also sets how rigorously hardware is analyzed and software developed.

facts.text: The booklet identifies IEC 61508, IEC 62061 and ISO 25119 as general alternatives to ISO 19014, but their fit was not verified.
facts.quote: The booklet names IEC 61508, IEC 62061 and ISO 25119 as general alternatives to ISO 19014 whose fit was not verified [Chapter 3]

facts.text: The booklet uses IEC 61508-3 tool classes T1 to T3 as a reference for qualifying tools, such as simulators, whose output becomes safety evidence.
facts.quote: uses the IEC 61508-3 tool classes T1 to T3 as a reference for qualifying tools, such as simulators, whose output becomes safety evidence [Chapters 12, 13]

facts.text: IEC 61508 practice uses a higher confidence level than ISO 26262 for proven-in-use claims.
facts.quote: notes that IEC 61508 practice uses a higher confidence level than ISO 26262 for proven-in-use claims [Chapter 10]

facts.text: The booklet's test allocation rule is software-in-the-loop (SIL) for volume and hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) for timing, interfaces and faults.
facts.quote: "SIL for volume, HIL for timing, interfaces and faults" [Chapter 1]

facts.text: When SIL appears in a sentence about test methods or benches, readers should interpret SIL as software-in-the-loop; when the sentence concerns required reliability, SIL means the safety grade.
facts.quote: A reading rule: if the sentence is about test methods or benches, SIL is software-in-the-loop; if it is about required reliability, it is the safety grade.

facts.text: Mining customers include "safety integrity" in their specifications.
facts.quote: mining customers write "safety integrity" into their specifications [Chapter 3].
